articles.title: MATERNAL HEALTH IS THE KEY
articles.description: AT 13 years of age, Sana was engaged to a cousin 10 years older than her. Marriage followed soon after. Naturally, the process of her physical and cognitive development was still in a crucial stage. Her father’s only source of income was small-scale farming, and she grew up stunted and undernourished. Poverty and uncertainty due to escalating climate events forced him to marry off his first daughter at an early age. Sana looked smaller, leaner and paler than standard at her age. Healthy eating and nutrition were unaffordable and often overlooked due to meagre resources, ignorance, or lack of education. At this undernourished stage before reaching adulthood, she was preparing to give birth to another life. With short stature and lean bodyweight, she and her child had to bear the consequences of early-marriage tradition. With rural maternal healthcare not available, she needed to travel a long, difficult journey to reach a hospital. This is the stark reality prevailing in rural Pakistan even though access to health services and adequate nutrition prevent complications and deficiencies, resulting in good cognitive development and strong immunity, which can help later in bearing a healthy new generation. The consequences of malnutrition among women of childbearing age are a significant challenge since Pakistan is facing an intergenerational cycle of malnutrition where malnourished mothers transfer severe deficiencies to their children. The triple burden of malnutrition includes underweight, obesity and micronutrient deficiencies, which are a threat to foetal stunting, low birthweight and chronic childhood anaemia. The consequences of teenage pregnancies with poor dietary habits include lower haemoglobin and calcium levels, causing iron deficiency anaemia or pre-eclampsia. Mothers receiving timely antenatal services in urban areas have more survival chances compared to mothers in rural or remote areas. Urban medical services facilitate vaccination, iron and folic acid supplementation, counselling for a balanced diet, and trained medical assistance during childbirth. These are all absent in rural areas. Sana’s vaccination and antenatal check-ups were delayed due to the long distance to the medical facility. Her financial and social constraints became a barrier to accessing timely antenatal medical care. Having healthy mothers in Pakistan today is the only way to ensure a healthy next generation, but the urban-rural disparity is making it just about impossible to meet the relevant targets. The World Health Organisation (WHO) in 2023 reported that the risk of maternal death in low-income countries was one in 66 compared to one in 8,000 in high-income countries. It is estimated that every dollar spent on maternal and infant health is an investment in human capital, helping build healthier communities and fostering economic growth, which is expected to generate $9 to $20 in return. The United Nations emphasised the need to address maternal and neonatal mortality as a matter of priority, reducing maternal mortality ratio (MMR) to 70 deaths per 100,000 live births, and neonatal mortality ratio (NMR) to 12 deaths per 1,000 live births to achieve Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 2030. About 20 per cent of preventable women’s death of child-bearing age occur due to maternal complications. In rural Pakistan, the MMR is 26pc higher than in urban areas due to distant medical health services. The gross domestic product (GDP) for healthcare in Pakistan is 0.8pc, and lacking health facilities near rural settings increases the risk for both the mother and the child. The barriers Sana faced were not only related to the absence of medical facilities alone; economic and social determinants were equally evident. After immense difficulty finding a sufficient form of public transport to the nearest health facility late in the night amid a heavy monsoon downpour, she was fortunate to reach the hospital, although complications due to her young age, under-nutritional status and nutritional deficiencies had already put her in the danger zone. She needed an urgent blood transfusion, while the newborn with low birthweight required close and additional monitoring for several days in an incubator. The lady doctor counselled Sana’s father, explaining to him the downside of early marriages. The pain and stress his daughter had suffered made the father vow that he would give his younger daughters enough time to grow healthy, learn and live a normal life. Sana also realised the relationship between a mother’s poor nutritional status and the fate of her child, and wished someone had told her earlier. The mother-baby dyad is a bond immensely intertwined even after the postpartum period. The umbilical cord is a connection that transfers not only nutrients during the pregnancy, but a connection that remains invisibly attached even after the pregnancy and throughout the phase of growth. As stunting starts long before a child is born, during pregnancy, an undernourished mother experiences maternal wasting, which causes babies to be born at a low gestational age, pointing towards early neonatal mortality and childhood wasting. Also, teenage pregnancies, with poor dietary habits, lower haemoglobin and calcium, can give rise to iron deficiency anaemia or pre-eclampsia. Investing in women’s health, nutrition and education is a strategic human capital investment, ensuring the sustainability and prosperity of the new generations. However, women in rural areas face inequality in accessing healthcare, wholesome or nourishing food, and education for healthier growth and survival. According to WHO 2025 data, Pakistan has made significant progress in alleviating this issue over the years. The MMR has declined from 276 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2006 to 155 in 2024. Likewise, the NMR has declined from 52 deaths per 1,000 live births to 37.6, and stillbirths from 39.8 per 1,000 births in 2000 to 27.5 in 2024. But the job is far from done. Micronutrient deficiencies are significantly associated with maternal health status and food insecurity. High inflation rates, poverty and lack of education compel rural girls/women to consume less nutritious, refined, and calorie-dense food to fill their stomachs, with no dietary diversity, causing deficiencies in iron, zinc, calcium and vitamins A, D and B12. The National Nutrition Survey (NNS) 2018 showed that one in seven women of reproductive age is undernourished. The urban and rural divide is clear; 15.8pc and 12pc, respectively. The same trend was seen in terms of iron and zinc insufficiency, leading to 8.4pc more cases of child stunting and 2.2pc more cases of child wasting than urban areas. This urban-rural disparity needs to be addressed on an urgent basis by focusing on medical care interventions alongside reforms related to girls’ education, awareness regarding health, balanced diet, sanitation and hygiene, and distribution of supplements like folic acid, iron and vitamin D in hard-to-reach areas. There should be equitable access to primary services. Lastly, government policies on early marriages and maternal health must be enforced, especially in rural areas, to ensure the welfare and prosperity of generations to come. The writer is Editor, Scientific Investigation and Global Network of Scientists (SIGNS).

articles.title: Scientists reveal the hidden instructions that build the human brain
articles.description: UCLA researchers have discovered two powerful influences that help guide how the human brain forms before birth. Radial glia, stem cells responsible for producing much of the cerebral cortex, change their behavior depending on how they process glucose and on physical contact with signals arriving from the thalamus. Those signals can alter which types of neurons are produced, including upper-layer neurons that are especially prominent in humans.

articles.title: The obesity-microbiome story is more complicated than ‘good’ and ‘bad’ bacteria
articles.description: This review finds that obesity is linked to reciprocal interactions between diet, the gut microbiome, microbial metabolites, and host metabolic pathways that influence appetite, insulin sensitivity, inflammation, and energy balance across the lifespan. It highlights diet as a particularly tractable way to influence this system, while emphasizing that microbiome changes associated with GLP-1 therapies remain difficult to separate from weight loss and that functional multi-omics approaches may help enable more personalized interventions.

articles.title: Act for Nutrition conference: Minister stresses need for communication, awareness to tackle malnutrition
articles.description: The second day of a two-day international conference, ‘Act For Nutrition: The Emergency We Can No Longer Ignore’, is being held at Islamabad’s Serena Hotel. The conference aims to address Pakistan’s persistent nutrition and stunting crisis. On the first day , experts at the conference warned that more than four in 10 children under five were stunted and malnutrition was costing Pakistan close to $17 billion annually. They also said that malnutrition was produced by a combination of poor diets, inadequate healthcare, weak water and sanitation services, poverty and other factors, making a multisectoral response essential. The two-day conference is bringing together policymakers, international development leaders, health professionals and nutrition experts to confront the burgeoning crisis and build momentum for urgent, coordinated action. View the full agenda here . 2:52pm - Minister says fathers must recognise a child’s nutrition as their responsibility Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said that public service messaging on nutrition must address the whole family, not just the mother. “Too often, we place the entire burden of a child’s nutrition on women, while decisions about food purchases, healthcare and women’s workloads may be taken by other members of the family. A mother cannot carry this responsibility alone,” he said. “Fathers must understand that nutrition is also their responsibility,” he said. 2:50pm - Minister calls for improving public service messaging Information Minister Attaullah Tarar highlighted the need for the right kind of messaging to tackle malnutrition. He said that communication could nutrition outcomes if it was done differently. “Public service messaging must move beyond telling people that malnutrition is a serious problem. Every message must give families practical steps they can take. Every message should have a result-oriented approach,” he said. He said that awareness programmes often focused on the problem rather than the solution. 2:44pm - Info minister says malnutrition not simply a health issues Information Minister Attaullah Tarar said that malnutrition was not simply a health issue. “It is a moral challenge, an economic imperative and a national emergency,” he said. The minister went on to say that malnutrition was shaped by maternal health, feeding practices, unsafe water, inadequate healthcare, climate vulnerabilities and unequal access to essential services. He further said that the Act for Nutrition conference should not be a one-off event, saying it should be an “action plan which we can implement throughout the year”. 2:40pm - Info minister stresses need for communication, awareness to tackle malnutrition Information Minister Attaullah Tarar, in his address, said that communication and awareness were essential for tackling malnutrition. He hailed DawnMedia group for raising awareness of the issue. He said that more than 40pc of children in Pakistan were stunted, while maternal mortality rate was 155 deaths per 100,000 live births. “Malnutrition costs Pakistan more than $17bn annually. If the right kind of strategy can be deployed across the country, the impact it would have on our gross domestic growth would benefit the common man,” he said. “Behind every stunted child is potential that may never be fully realised. Behind every malnourished mother is a family at greater risk. And behind every year of inaction is another generation beginning life at a disadvantage,” he said. 2:00pm - Lunch break 1:40pm - UK expert stresses need for safely managed water and sanitation Oliver Cumming, the environmental health lead at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said: “The prospect of safely managed water and sanitation in Pakistan is not something which can be achieved tomorrow, and it is not as simple as shifting gears that you go from basic to safely managed.” However, he suggested that recognition towards the goal could lead to universal access to safely managed WASH services sooner rather than later. “We have to be realistic that it will not happen tomorrow, but putting in place the investment, the political arguments [...] universal access to safely managed services can become possible within a decade,” he added. “This is where we need to get if we really want to solve the problem of chronic malnutrition.” 1:25pm - Expert says water quality a ‘big issue’ for Pakistan Dr Saima Khan — a water, sanitation and hygiene policy specialist — called for targeting the 36 districts in the country contributing to stunting in children. She said that WASH infrastructure investments should be done in these districts. She also said that water quality was a “big issue” for Pakistan. She said that the country’s northern areas, Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan had no infrastructure for sanitation or sewerage. She said that this was deteriorating the quality of drinking water in these areas. 1:05pm - WB official calls for understanding WASH-related drivers of malnutrition Senior water specialist at the World Bank, Basharat Saeed, underscored the significance of gaining a “sophisticated understanding” of WASH-related drivers behind child malnutrition. “You need to look at what are the processes at a given location that are leading to the accumulation of faecal waste, accumulation in a way that it is exposing sensitive ecosystem and exposing people to faecal pathogens,” Saeed said. He added that it should also be made possible to track the common pathways for oral transmission for faecal material. “If you can map that out at the start of a programme design, then you know what sort of WASH investment is needed,” he said, stressing the need for a sophisticated understanding of WASH-related drivers of malnutrition. He added that as a result of adopting such an approach, the “proposed solution will also become slightly more comprehensive”. Senior water specialist at the World Bank, Basharat Saeed, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim 12:49pm - UK expert says water and sanitation alone cannot end stunting Oliver Cumming, the environmental health lead at the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine, said that water and sanitation alone cannot end stunting, but it was essential part of the comprehensive strategies needed to address it. He said that for the water and sanitation sector, nutrition was often peripheral, adding that this needed to change. He said that 20pc of children in South Asia were stunted at birth, highlighting the need for prevention and an integrated approach to the issue. 12:45pm - WaterAid official calls for moving towards delivering multisectoral approach Country director at WaterAid, Mian Muhammad Junaid, stressed that the conversation on a multisectoral approach needed to move beyond talking and towards financing and delivering results. “We are working in silos; we still tend to organise ourselves in sectors, where nutrition sits in one policy sector, health in another, water and sanitation somewhere else, climate separately, social protection is another,” Junaid said. He went on to note that a child did not experience these boundaries; rather, it was a lived reality for them. “This is where I think Pakistan needs to move from talking about a multisectoral approach to actually financing and delivering one,” he added. 12:41pm - WaterAid official says child’s environment important for addressing malnutrition In his keynote speech, Mian Muhammad Junaid, the country director for WaterAid, raised alarm at the impact of lack of water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) services on a child’s development and nutrition. “A child cannot be well nourished if the environment in which the child grows is making them sick,” he said. He said WASH services were often an “important but missed” aspect of addressing malnutrition. “WASH is a part of nutrition,“ Junaid said. “A child may receive the right food, nutritional counselling, cash transfer and access to health facilities, but if the child is repeatedly exposed to contaminated drinking water, faecal contamination, poor sanitation and an unhealthy environment, we are asking that child to grow and develop against very difficult odds,” he said. Mian Muhammad Junaid, the country director for WaterAid, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim 12:40pm - Panel discussion on contribution of dirty water, poor sanitation to stunting begins A panel discussion on how dirty water and poor sanitation contribute to stunting has now begun. 12:38pm - BISP official says policies, legislation remain ‘only on paper’ Tehmina Gulzar, the deputy director of nutrition at the Benazir Income Support Programme, said that hygiene, agricultural, sanitation sectors had to come together to respond to malnutrition. She said that BISP had trained doctors, paramedical staff and teachers on adolescent nutrition to bring knowledge to communities. She also said that while policies and legislation were drafted, they were “only on paper”. “We need to bring them into practice. All sectors are working on [nutrition], but they are fragmented efforts,” she said, highlighting the need for the digital integration of all sectors. 12:31pm - Expert says malnutrition not ‘poverty-related’ Dr Farhana Memon, the programme director of Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal and Child Health, dispelled the perception that malnutrition was tied to poverty. “It is said that malnutrition is just poverty-related; I don’t think so. I have been in the field for 27 years, and whenever I ask a woman what she has eaten for breakfast, she will tell me she had tea and rusk,” Dr Memon said. “We have failed to convince her that she can get an egg for the same cost,” she said. “Let’s take an example of two issues in public health — breastfeeding and micronutrient deficiencies — these are not poverty-related; it’s knowledge-related,” she said. 12:15pm - BISP official says social protection programmes can play ‘significant role’ in improving nutrition outcomes Tehmina Gulzar, the deputy director of nutrition at the Benazir Income Support Programme, said that social protection programmes can play a “significant role” in improving nutrition outcomes. She added that BISP was a very good example of how social protection programmes could contribute toward human capital development. She also said that BISP had a huge collection of data that could be used by different sectors involved in addressing nutrition. Tehmina Gulzar, the deputy director of nutrition at the Benazir Income Support Programme, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim 12:01pm - Expert says nutrition cannot be viewed in isolation CEO of the Pakistan Alliance on Early Childhood Development Khadija Khan warned against viewing nutrition in isolation. “Because for holistic development, you need a complete package and that package is described in the nurturing care framework, which is talking about good health, adequate nutrition, responsive caregiving, safety, security and early learning opportunity.” She held that until and unless these inputs were met, it was not possible to achieve holistic child development. “We do talk about a multisectoral approach and an integrated approach, but still the families are knocking on different doors for different services. In reality, we do not really give integrated services to our children,” Khan added. 11:49am - Non-profit head says people do not ‘believe in the system’ Shahid Lone, the chairman of the Allah Walay Foundation, said that if policymakers and those responsible for implementation did not put their “soul” into what they were doing, then what they were aiming for “would never work”. He acknowledged that his take was more “philosophical”. He highlighted that government officials say one thing on stage and another when they are behind the scenes. “We have policies, we have departments, but we have people who do not believe in the system,” he said. He questioned how those who did not have vision or believed in their work could implement policies. Shahid Lone, the chairman of the Allah Walay Foundation, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim 11:37am - ‘Behaviour of healthcare providers pathetic’ Dr Farhana Memon, the programme director of Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal and Child Health, also criticised the behaviour of healthcare workers. “The behaviour of healthcare providers is pathetic,” Dr Memon said, noting that most healthcare workers did not counsel patients on family planning, nutrition, or vaccination. “We have been trying to change the behaviour of the community for the past decade, but now it is time to change the behaviour of healthcare providers.” “If a person or a woman comes into contact with you, please don’t waste the opportunity,” she urged. 11:34am - Expert decries lack of dedicated funding for nutrition Programme director of Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal, and Child Health Dr Farhana Memon decried the lack of funds to address malnutrition. “If you want to [translate] policies into action, you should have some cost,” she said, adding that donors largely funded efforts to end malnutrition. “This is not the solution,” Memon remarked, adding that nutrition should be treated as a separate entity. She further urged that the government must utilise every access point as an opportunity to counsel families about nutrition. Programme director of Reproductive, Maternal, Neonatal, and Child Health Dr Farhana Memon speaks at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Muhammad Asim 11:25am - Session on multisectoral approach to nutrition begins A session on the multisectoral approach to nutrition has now begun. 11:20am - KP CM says govt working on addressing malnutrition Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi, in a video message, said that facilitation centres were being established to address malnutrition among pregnant women and young children. He said that the provincial government, under PTI founder Imran Khan’s vision, was working on this issue and others. He ended by thanking DawnMedia for highlighting malnutrition and other social issues. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Chief Minister Sohail Afridi’s video message at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 11:10am - Govt official calls for cohesive national narrative on malnutrition Dr Shabana Haider, member (population) in the Planning Commission of Pakistan, stressed the need for a cohesive national narrative in addressing malnutrition. “Do not go switching your national narrative; sometimes it is said that two kids are enough, sometimes it is one, and sometimes you ask women to time their pregnancies. Please develop a narrative that you can lead on and that everybody — from development partners to private sector — can converge on,” she said. 11:00am - Govt official says nutritional challenges cannot be addressed without acknowledging population dynamics Dr Shabana Haider, member (population) in the Planning Commission of Pakistan, said that nutritional challenges could not be addressed without acknowledging population dynamics and demographic dividends could not be reaped without investing in nutrition. She said that while Pakistan had done a lot on the policy side, the documents themselves were not enough. “We are very good at framing policies ... sorry, excuse me, this has to change ... let’s all recognise that our priority has not been population,” she said, adding that population had been neglected as a subject. 10:50am - KP govt official says malnutrition, family planning interlinked Dr Fazal Majeed, the director of nutrition at the Directorate General Health Services for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, said that Pakistan had a stunting growth rate of 40pc, adding that it was 48pc in KP’s merged districts. He also said that almost 40pc of women of reproductive age were also anaemic, calling the figures “alarming”. “Malnutrition, family planning ... are interlinked,” he said. He said some of the barriers in KP were fragmented delivery points, geographical and security-related. Dr Fazal Majeed, the director of nutrition at the Directorate General Health Services for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference, — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:35am - Public health professional says history of Pakistan’s health programmes ‘one of isolation’ Dr Talib Lashari, a public health professional with the Sindh government’s health department, said that the nexus between nutrition and family planning was “well established but poorly practised in Pakistan”. “The history of Pakistan’s public health programmes and initiatives is one of isolation. All the programmes have been well-designed and, to some extent, properly funded, but they were implemented in isolation,” he said. 10:24am - Govt adviser says nutrition needs to be reclassified as a capital expenditure Adnan Pasha Siddiqui, the adviser to the minister of finance, said that nutrition needed to be reclassified as a capital expenditure rather than as an expense. “So this single accounting decision suppresses the investment narrative permanently ... these are fundamental flaws we need to correct,” he said. Adnan Pasha Siddiqui, the adviser to the minister of finance, addresses the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 10:17am - Govt adviser says lack of investment in nutrition hurts Pakistan’s GDP Adnan Pasha Siddiqui, the adviser to the minister of finance, said that burgeoning population and lack of resources were a “collective failure of capital investment”. “We are reflecting everything nutrition-related as a health expenditure ... every rupee that is withheld from a pregnant women’s diet is a deduction from the country’s gross domestic product in the future,” he said. He said that in the country, nutrition was divided across several sectors. Siddiqui said that the annual loss from malnutrition was $17bn. He said that in South Asia, labour productivity was suppressed because of nutrition. “And it is a structural liability to our sovereign credit profile,” he said. 10:08am - World Bank official says nutrition is viewed through ‘a human capital lens’ Sara Shahzad, the senior health specialist from the World Bank, said that the group had 10-year country partnership framework with the government of Pakistan focused on six priority areas, one of which was stunting reduction. “So the way the World Bank looks at population stabilisation and nutrition, specifically the stunting agenda, is through a human capital lens,” she said. Talking about stunting, she said that 30-40pc of it occurred before a child was born. “So, the first 1,000 days are absolutely critical but also the adolescence period,” she said. Sara Shahzad, the senior health specialist from the World Bank, speaks at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 9:58am - Expert highlights ‘experimentation’ in Pakistan’s population planning Dr Ali Mir, the country director for the Population Council, said that there was always a tendency in Pakistan of “making the same mistakes again and again”. Talking about Pakistan’s previous population reforms, he highlighted wavering political commitment and policy inconsistency. “We never explicitly had a population policy till 2002. It was always couched in development planning,” he said. He said that due to this, Pakistan was constantly “experimenting”. Dr Mir said that now things were moving in the right direction, with the establishment of the Population Council. Dr Ali Mir, the country director for the Population Council, speaks at the Act for Nutrition conference. — White Star/Tanveer Shahzad 9:55am - Doctor says nutrition is ‘not an isolated event’ Dr Saima Hamid, the programme and research lead at the Population Council, said that Pakistan’s population growth rate is at 2.55pc. She said that in 28 years, the country’s population would double, putting a huge burden on resources. “This clearly is a challenge of not just the quantity but also the quality of diet. We need to ensure that diverse nutrition reaches those most vulnerable,” she said. She also said that Pakistan’s domestic food security was on the decline, adding that “nutrition is not just an isolated event”. “One sector isn’t really responsible ... there is a clear intersection of nutrition, food security, health, purchasing power,” she said. 9:52am - Session on population and resources has begun A session on how a nation cannot feed, educate or employ what it cannot count on sustaining has now begun. 9:50am - 2nd day of conference begins The second day of the conference begins with a short film titled Leaky Guts from the Aga Khan University.
